records.our_prose: Sweet potatoes are a warm-weather crop grown for the sweet, starchy roots that form underground. Despite the name, they are not related to regular potatoes; they belong to the morning glory family. You do not grow them from seed or from tubers. Instead you plant slips, which are rooted sprouts, set out only after all frost is past and the soil is warm. The plants send out long, trailing vines that cover the ground, so they are grown on ridges or mounds with plenty of room. Sweet potatoes need a long, hot summer (about 3 to 4 months of warm, frost-free weather) and they love heat, so the warm South, Gulf, Florida, and the desert Southwest are the best places to grow them, while cooler northern gardens are a stretch and use black plastic and fast varieties. Go easy on fertilizer, especially nitrogen, or you get lots of vine and few sweet potatoes. Dig the crop before the first frost, which kills the vines, then cure the roots somewhere warm and humid for a week or two, which heals the skins and makes them sweet, and store them warm, around 55 to 60°F. Never put sweet potatoes in the fridge or anywhere cold, which ruins them. This is the opposite of how you store regular potatoes. The young leaves are also good to eat as a cooked green.

records.source_context: Moist-fleshed varieties of sweet potato are often called “yams.” However, sweet potatoes are not true yams, which belong to a different plant family, called Dioscoreaceae. Sweet potatoes belong to the morning glory family (Convolvulaceae) and are related to morning glory and field bind weed. True yams are rarely found in local grocery stores, vary greatly in size, need a very long, warm growing season, and are commonly grown only in the tropics.

records.our_prose: Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) is a warm-season, frost-tender member of the morning glory family (Convolvulaceae), not a nightshade and unrelated to the ordinary potato despite the shared name. It is grown for its swollen storage roots and planted not from seed or tubers but from slips: rooted sprouts pulled from a bedded seed root and set out only after all frost danger has passed and the soil is warm, above about 65°F. The plant is a vigorous, sprawling groundcover, running long vines that root at the nodes, and it is grown on raised ridges or mounds that drain well and give the roots room to expand. The crop needs a long, hot season, roughly 90 to 120 frost-free days, and it relishes the summer heat that stalls many other vegetables, so the warm South, Gulf, Florida, and the low deserts are its stronghold while short-season northern gardens are marginal and lean on black plastic and fast varieties. Feed sparingly and keep nitrogen low, since rich ground grows rampant vine and few roots. The crop is dug before the first frost, which kills the vines, then cured warm and humid (about 80 to 85°F at high humidity for one to two weeks) to heal the skins and turn starch to sugar, and stored warm, near 55 to 60°F. Sweet potatoes are damaged by cold and must never be refrigerated or stored below about 50 to 55°F, the opposite of white potato storage. The young leaves and shoots are also edible as a cooked green.

records.source_context: Although it has been found associated with several genera, its primary hosts are in the genus Ipomoea . Among vegetable crops, only sweet potato, Ipomoea batatas , is a suitable host. Native plants can be important hosts of sweetpotato weevil. Railroad vine, Ipomoea pescaprae , and morning glory, Ipomoea panduratea , are among the suitable wild hosts.

records.our_prose: Sweet potatoes are light feeders and specifically want restrained nitrogen. University of Georgia suggests working in about 30 pounds of 5-10-10 per 1,000 square feet before planting, then side-dressing roughly 4 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 feet of row about 4 to 6 weeks after transplanting. Favor a low-nitrogen, higher-potassium ratio: too much nitrogen (and fresh manure) grows lush, sprawling vine and few storage roots, while adequate potassium supports root sizing and quality.

records.source_context: For more information on diseases and control, see HGIC 2214, Irish & Sweetpotato Diseases . Harvest Sweetpotatoes should be ready to harvest about 90 to 120 days after planting. Harvest the sweetpotatoes when 30 percent of the roots are larger than 3½ inches in diameter.

records.our_prose: The sweet potato weevil (Cylas formicarius, family Brentidae). Larvae do the principal damage by mining tunnels through the storage roots (and stems), leaving them riddled with cavities, spongy, and darkened; the feeding induces bitter terpenes even at low levels. It breeds continuously in warm climates, spreads mainly on infested slips and in leftover roots, and continues to damage the crop in storage.

records.our_prose: Small holes and dark, spongy tunnels running through the storage roots, found when you dig or cut them. Even light feeding triggers a chemical reaction that gives the roots a bitter taste and an off, turpentine-like odor, ruining them for eating. The adult is a slender, ant-like weevil, about a quarter inch long, with a dark head and snout, reddish legs, and a metallic blue-black body; you may see chewing on stems and leaves. This is the single most serious pest of sweet potato, worst in the Deep South and Gulf.

records.our_prose: Wireworms are click beetle larvae that live in the soil for several years and are most numerous in ground recently in sod, grass, or corn. The same root-scarring complex includes larvae of spotted and banded cucumber beetles (Diabrotica) and flea beetles (Systena), which move into the soil to feed on the developing roots through the season.

records.source_context: Sweetpotato plants often compensate for early season wireworm damage by forming a callous skin over the feeding site, often causing irregular root development. Crop rotation for wireworm. As some wireworm species can persist in the soil for several years as larvae, long-term crop rotation away from suitable host plants is one of the most effective methods to reduce the risk of root damage.

records.our_prose: On the Florida peninsula, sweet potato is a warm-season crop planted from spring through June (UF/IFAS: anytime after frost through the end of June; about 120 to 150 days), with the heat-loving vines running through the hot, humid summer and harvest from summer into fall. In frost-free deep South Florida, plantings can be staggered over a long window for a harvest across much of the year. The sweet potato weevil and root-knot nematode are the key concerns, so certified slips and rotation matter. records.our_prose: Sweet potatoes are grown from slips: rooted sprouts pulled from a bedded seed root, not from seed and not from seed-potato-style pieces. Buy certified, disease-free and weevil-free slips, or bed a healthy root in warm, moist medium about 6 weeks ahead and pull the sprouts once they have roots. Set slips 3 to 4 inches deep with two or more nodes buried, spacing them 12 to 18 inches apart on ridges or mounds in rows 3 to 4 feet apart, once all frost danger has passed and the soil is above about 65°F (70 to 80°F is better). There is no indoor seed-starting step; the slip itself is the transplant. In short-season areas, planting through black plastic warms the soil and buys extra growing days.

records.our_prose: Sweet potatoes want even, moderate moisture, especially while the slips establish and again while the storage roots are sizing. Aim for about 1 inch of water per week including rain, delivered in deeper, less frequent soakings. Once well established the deep root system makes them fairly drought tolerant, but a prolonged dry-then-wet swing during root bulking causes cracked and misshapen roots. Ease off water in the last few weeks before harvest so the roots do not split and the skins firm up.
